description: In 1866, Raskolnikov kills a pawnbroker to prove that he is a superman. Dostoyevsky turns the crime into a laboratory of conscience and redemption.

hero.hook: A murder committed for the sake of a theory. And a conscience that will not forgive.

blocks.text: Published in **1866**, **[[Crime and Punishment]]** is one of the greatest novels of **Fyodor Dostoyevsky**. **Rodion Raskolnikov**, a poor student in **Saint Petersburg**, commits a double murder believing that he is defending an abstract idea. Far more than a psychological thriller, the book explores guilt, **nihilism**, and the chance of a spiritual rebirth.

Dostoyevsky does not simply tell the story of a crime. He turns it into a laboratory where an intellectual theory smashes into the reality of a human conscience. The novel asks a question that still burns: can you kill in the name of a higher idea?

Dostoyevsky wrote the novel deep in debt and under pressure from his publisher. In **1849**, as a member of the **[[Petrashevsky Circle]]**, he faced a mock execution by firing squad on **Semyonovsky Square**, then left for the **[[Omsk Fortress]]** in Siberia and four years of hard labor. That brush with death changed the way he saw the world.

blocks.caption: Fyodor Dostoyevsky, novelist of conscience and suffering

blocks.text: Dostoyevsky burned a first draft written in the first person, then started again in the third person to gain narrative distance.

Back from exile, he fought **[[Russian nihilism of the 1860s]]**, the intellectual movement that rejected every moral and religious authority in the name of reason and science. **Crime and Punishment** shows how an idea cut off from real life and from love can lead to murder. Raskolnikov is not a monster: he is a brilliant intellectual who takes himself for a superman.

sections.title: The author at the edge: life and context

blocks.text: Raskolnikov splits humanity into the “ordinary” and the “extraordinary.” The second group, men like **Napoleon**, would have the right to break the moral law for a higher purpose. To test his theory he kills an old pawnbroker whom he judges useless and harmful to society, with an axe borrowed from the caretaker.

blocks.caption: Saint Petersburg in the 19th century: poverty and intellectual fever

blocks.text: The crime goes wrong: he also kills **Lizaveta**, the old woman's innocent sister, who walks in on the murder. He never uses the stolen money, which he hides under a rock. Raskolnikov discovers that he is not the superman he thought he was: his conscience cannot bear the blood, and fever eats him alive.

sections.title: The temptation of the superman: Raskolnikov's theory

blocks.text: The “punishment” starts with the murder itself, long before any courtroom. Raskolnikov shuts himself away, unable to bear the presence of his mother **Pulcheria** or his sister **Dunya**. The magistrate **Porfiry Petrovich**, a master of **[[Forensic psychology]]**, knows he is guilty but lets him accuse himself.

Facing him stands **Sonia Marmeladova**, a young woman pushed into prostitution to feed her family. She reads him the story of the **[[Resurrection of Lazarus]]** and opens a path that is not rational at all: confession and love. Where Raskolnikov rose through intellectual pride, she lowered herself through love of other people.

The epilogue in Siberia shows **[[Redemption through suffering]]** as something slow and difficult. Raskolnikov does not drop his theory of the superman at once, but Sonia's love slowly cracks his intellectual shell. **Nietzsche** would later recognize in Dostoyevsky an extraordinary psychologist of guilt and transgression.

The novel still burns today: can you kill in the name of an abstract idea, of a “great cause”? Dostoyevsky answers that the human conscience always ends up claiming what it is owed, and that real rebirth comes through humiliation and love, not through reason alone.
**Crime and Punishment** shows intellectual pride failing against moral reality. Raskolnikov's real punishment is not prison, it is the isolation of his soul.

sections.title: Resurrection, and the legacy of a total novel
